0.1 This Indian Standard ( Part II) was adopted by the Indian Standards Insritunon on 26 February 1979, after the draft finalized by the Nutrition
Sectional Committee had been approved by the Agricultural and Food Products Division Council. 0.2 The groundnut is by far the largest oilseed crop in India with a share of over half the total oil seeds produced. Some part of the groundnuts produced are consumed directly, and a large proportion is used for the expression of oil in village GHANIS, screw presses or solvent-extraction uruts. The 011 is used in India in unrefined or refined form, and the cake or solvent-extracted meal is exported in huge quantities. 0.3 In 1960, it was discovered that the common mould Aspergtllus flalJus could grow on groundnuts and groundnut cakes to produce highly-toxic materrals, the aflatoxins In young animals which are at a stage of rapid growth, these toxins mterfere with cell division and Cause death. In older animals, mcludmg man, they are unphcated in liver cirrhosis, and possibly in cancer. As a result, very low permissible levels of aflatoxin for oilcakes and edible flours have been laid down in many countries. Apart from nutritional implications, there are economic ones also since exported cakes or flours can be rejected if the prescribed levels of aflatOXIOS are exceeded. 0.4 The major danger of mould infestation occurs during the harvesting and drying of groundnuts rn the field, and their subsequent storage in the warehouse or MANDl. Accordingly IS: 9071 (Part I ).1979* is being issued simultaneously WIth this standard which gives specific recommendations to minimize mould attack and toxin development in groundnuts at all stages prior to purchase of seed by the user. IS: 56861970t give> detailed directives for sou nd procedures applicable to oilseeds in general.
.Code of practice for control of aflatoxin in groundnuu Part I Harvesung, transport and storage of groundnut kernels. 1'Code of practice for haudlmg and storage of OIlseeds,

3

IS t 9071 ( Part II ) - 1979 0.5 IS: 44-27-1967� provides useful guidelines to general quality for
purchase of groundnuts. The specific suggestions given In this document are for buying nuts of high quality, with a good storage potential, as judged in terms various indicators. Once groundnuts are bought dunng the main arrival season, they may have to be stored in the oil mills for periods as long as even nine months before processing. Mould infestation can eavily develop during such storage unless precautions are taken Groundnuts can be processed through a screw press or expeller to yield crude groundnut oil and an oilcake. If the crude oil is subsequently alkali refined and bleached, aflatoxms should be totally eliminated In India, however, a considerable proportion of the groundnut 011 is used for cookmg in the raw form. It has been shown that 10�20 percent of the toxins In the nuts pass into the raw oil, which may, therefore, carry high levels of aflatoxin, posmg a considerable health hazard.

or

0.6 This standard Kives directives for each of these user stages. Criteria
are laid down for the purchase of groundnuts. Next, measures desrg ned to control the level of aflatoxin during seed storage at the oil mill are outlined. This is followed by steps [0 reduce the aflatoxin level in the starting materral prior to its processing by suitable sorting and preprocessing of the nuts themselves. Such operations are always necessary to ensure oilcake of good quality, and are especially important when the resulting meal has to be of a quality suitable for human consumption, as defined in the three standards IS: 4684-1975t. IS: 4875-1975~ and IS : 8'212-1976�. Procedures for the reduction of aflatoxin in crude groundnut oil both at an industrial level lind on a domestic scale have been suggested.

0.7 In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from The Oil Technological Research Institute, An antapur and The Protein Foods and Nutrinon Development Association of India, Bombay

0.8 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this
standard is complied With, the final value, observed 01 calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance With IS: 2-196011. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

I. SCOPE
1.1 This standard r Part II) recommends methods for the control of aflatoxi.n duri~g the Luying of groundnuts, their storage, and their processmg to oilcake or edrble flours, and durin... the treatment of raw groundnut oil prior to edible use "

2. TERMINOLOGY
2.0 FOT the purpose of this standard the following definitions shall apply. 2.1 Bags - Jute bags with oilseeds, weighing approximately 90 kg. 2.2 Food Category - The type of nuts where the oil is to be used without further refining or the meal is intended for human consumpnon. 2.3 Feed Category - The type of nuts where the oil is to be refined or the meal is intended for use as an animal feed.
2.4 PUCCA Room ventilators,

Room with sound flooring, roof, walls and

3. BUYING GROUNDNUTS
3.1 End Use - In the case of groundnuts of Food Category, particular care has to be taken in the choice of ground nuts. Buying of Hand-picked Selected (H PS) kernels and their immediate processing is strongly recommended, In the case of groundnuts of Feed Category a slightly greater tolerance is possible, though care In buymg is still desirable. 3.2 Groundnut Kernel Quality - Guideli nes for the purchase of groundnut kernels under both categories are shown in Table 1. 3.3 Other Oilseed. - The groundnut kernels should also be free from non-edrble oilseeds, in particular such tOXIC oilseeds as castor, MAHUA and argemone.

4. STORAGE OF NUTS AT PROCESSING POINT
".1 Storage Strudure - A separate PUCCA room with high ceiling, sound floorrng, mesh-protected Windows and, if possible, exhaust fans would greatly assist sound groundnut storage. If this is not possible, a cemented floor, and a sloping roof of galvanized sheets with sufficient overhang to fully protect the seeds from rain or bird dropprngs, is desirable. If only storage in the open is possible, the minimum require-ment is spread plastic sheets to ensure that there is no direct contact with the ground, and complete covering of the piles of bags or of loose seeds with plastic sheets or tarpaulins.

4.2 Cleaniug and Sprayiug of Storage Structure - Before the start of the season, and perrodrcally thereafter, the storage srruct ure or area should be thoroughly cleaned and swept down, and all trash, spillage and grains which are thus collected should be burnt, burred or removed far away since they are rich In lrve insects, eg-gs and moulds. The area and the walls should be thoroughly sprayed wirh an emulsified residual insecticide, such as 03 percent lindane, or 3 percent malathion at the rate of 5 litres per 100 mi. The ground surroundmg the buildmg to a distance of about 2 rn, or the ground used for storage, should also be similarly sprayed. For outdoor treatment 5 percent DDT as wettable powder should be used while for indoor treatment lindane and malathion are preferable. G

IS : 9071 ( Part II ) � 1979 4.3 Bagging of Groundnut!l- Groundnuts m shell ( pods) store much
better than inner kernels, and the added protection over long storage periods is worth the extra bulk and room needed. If either pods or nuts are bought loose, they should be bazged pnor to storage, and the bags used for this purpose should be made Insect-free by Sill table fUlmgalIOli treaunenr, such as t'''pmure to methyl bromide-et hy lene dibrorrude mixture, In air-tight enclosures or chambers After fillmg wuh pods or nuts, the bags should be folded over and stitched or sealed to prevent sprllage. 4.4 Stacking of Bags - It is advantageous La permanently mark the stacking design on the ground with white pam t. A distance of 1 m fi om the walls, and between the stacks, should be left free to provide corrrdors for free pa<sage of workmen wrthdra wing bags, inspectors, a nd sprayers, The stacking should not be done On the floor but on wooden pallets ( platforms constructed of wooden strrps nailed down at light angles ). The stacks should not be [00 big or too 11Igh. A lO-m square, 3'metre high stack has several ad vantages. The stack, may be built up round a central open space which should act as a chrrnney for hot au to move upwards, thus drawrng III cold air by convection from below to promote coohng. Provisron of exhaust f.1n; at the top of the storage room will augment coolmg. 4.5 FUll1igation - After the bag'S art> stacked, particul.n ly at the begmnmg of the season , anv revuieu t mfecrron should bl' destroyed by enclosing the bags 111 a sheet of tarpaulin or other ;turdy plavt.ic matenal and exposmg the pill" to Iurmganrs such as met hy I bromide ( 48 !,;/ma ) for 36 hours or methyl bromide-ethylene dibromide (24 g/m 3 ) for 36 hours It I' advantageous to pre\ ent crosv-infevratron dur)ll~ subsequent storage by spraying the 'tacks every 3 months u-ing l md ane , malathion or pvret hi um sprav forrnu latrous. If the atmospheric temperature d urmg Iumiz auon I' abnv e ~O�C, I t I ' more effccnve and economical to Iurrugate with a mixture or me thy I bromide and ethv lene dibr orrude than methyl bromide alone. 4.6 Continuous Monitoring - Many serious problems ran be forestalled bv regular inspectron. The external relarive hu rmdity Will determine the seed moisture level, which should be below a cr mcal value, for swrage WIthollt loss of qualrty. Stnps OT paper dned ah er dippmg 111 0 I percent aqueous cobalt thtocyanate solution, If placed at several places III the stacks, Will remain blue below a rclanve hurruditv of 70 percent, and turn pink when this level IS exceeded This will mdicate that the groundnuts III the VICinity run the fisk of mould mf. station. Hot 'pots, caused by local seed overheating, should be located and the batch of seed processed at once. Periodically seeds should be Withdrawn ... t random uSllIg a metal seed sampler, spht open, and exarnmed for fungus patches or brown discoloured spots caused by mould. These seeds should be utilIzed at once, but no! used for manufacture of edible protem product,

S. PROCESSJNG OF GROUNDNUTS TO PROTEIN AND OIL
COMPONENTS
5.1 Sortiog -Where an edible flour is to be made, the buying of HPS kernels and their processing as soon as possible may be economical. If pods are bought, they shall carry kernels of very high quality. The first step is then to decorticate the pods by any suitable process, followed by removal of debris by shaker screens or by air blowmg.
5.1.1 The kernels in their skins are next subject to sorting, the purpose of which is to remove shrrvelied, mouldy or drscoloured nuts which often carry high levels of toxins. This operanon can be done manually by inspectIng the red nuts as they pa~s along a moving belt. Alternatively photoelectric sortin~ machines, which discard all nuts which are nonuruforrn may be employed. The kernels are then subject to mild roasting (blanching), after which the skins become friable and loose. When the nuts are sphr, the germs or cuticles also get detached. During roavnng, several sigm of nut deterioration should be watched for, such a! unusual d.irkening of the red skin, browning of the kernels themselves, and special resistance to nut sphtung. The checking of random samples for aflatoxm content at thrs stage should provide useful pointers to subsequent treatment of the nuts 5.1.2 Dilution of nuts of very low toxin level with those of higher level to brmg the final products WIthin specification limits should never be done. Nuts rejected during sorting procedures should not be used for manufacture of protein products meant for human use. Roasting loosens the skins and makes them friable, besides enabling easy snlnting of the nuts and detaching of the ger ms, Split sorted nuts should be freed of red skins and germs by blowing, screening. vibrauon, separation or other means. Manual sorting of roasted nuts after splitting on a moving belt under ultraviolet light (with proper precautions to protect the eyes of the workers) is very efficacrous, since spots of mould show up dearly as a blue, gr",en or y"'llow fluorescence.

5:2 Removal of Skins and Germs -

5.3 OU Expressioo - Oil may be removed from the cleaned groundnut kernels by the usual method of screw-pressmg, which may be followed by subsequent solvent-extraction, or by integrated processing which employs aqueous systems and cencri fugal separation. Strict cleanliness and hygiene shall be maintained dunng these operations,

6. TRE.\TMENT OF CAKE AND OIL
6.1 Treatment of Cake - The resulting cake if derived from nuts of Food Category is likely to be of edible quality. If the cake when made conforms to such quality, especially in regard to aflatoxin level, no

IS I 9071 ( Part II ) � 1979
further treatment is desirable. If marginally higher than the limit, the cake may be treated with ammonia gas under slight pressure, or with ozone, to reduce aflatoxin to very low levels.

6.1.1 The resulting cake may also be used for preparation of edible protein Isolate by solubilization in alkali, precipitation wuh acid, centrifugation, washing with water and drying. During the alkali solubilization step, aflatoxin may be destroyed by treatment with hydrogen peroxide in suitable strength and quantity, after which the excess reagent is destroyed by adding the enzyme catalase. This should onlv be done when the level of aflatoxin is marginally higher than the limit, since use of the excess oxidising agent required to destroy high aflatoxin levels also tends to destroy protein quality. 6.1.2 Sodium hypochlorite may also be similarly employed to destroy aflatoxin.
6.2 Tl"eatment of Oil - Standard industrial procedures of alkali refining totally destroy afiatoxm, particularly if further followed bv bleaching and deodorisanon of tbe o i], For oil which IS not thus refined, filtration through a special type filter cloth in place of the filter press cloth now used has been found effective in lowering aflatoxin levels to a safe limit. A procedure for use in the home is to heat the raw groundnut oil to 80DC and wash it when hot with 4 rimes it own volu me of 10 percent sodium chloride (salt) solution, by which the aflatoxin level should be greatly reduced and the oil should be safer to use. Exposure of oil in 10 ern layer co strong sunlight for 15 minutes or in a glass bottle for 1 hour should also greatly reduce the aflatoxin level
